title: Margaret Hamilton has died
titleZh: 玛格丽特·汉密尔顿去世
author: muglug
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Margaret Hamilton, a profoundly influential computer scientist best known for leading the software engineering team at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab during NASA’s Apollo program, died on Sep. 30. She was 90.A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline. She worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, after which she became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO.Her life’s work was recognized with many awards and honors, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama, whose citation noted: “Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon.”“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” says Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Margaret Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success. And for her that was just the beginning! She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.”Early life and projects at MITBorn in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958. She moved to Boston, Massachusetts, in 1959 with her husband while he pursued a law degree. Hamilton soon found a temporary position in the meteorology department at MIT, working with professor of meteorology Edward N. Lorenz SM ’43, ScD ’48 on weather prediction software. This was her first entry point into computer programming, and her work would go on to inform Lorenz’s future publications on chaos theory.From there, Hamilton took a role as a programmer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States’ first air defense system. Hamilton wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer (XD-1), used by the U.S. Air Force to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time.In 1965 Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw an advertisement in the newspaper: The Instrumentation Lab at MIT was seeking people to develop software to “send man to the moon.” The lab had won the contract from NASA to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project. Hamilton worked first on the software for the uncrewed Apollo missions and then was promoted into leading the team developing the on-board flight software for the crewed missions. By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software. “From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s. Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”“Defensive” programming and priority-driven software take humans to the moonHamilton discovered a talent for leadership, as well as a keen instinct for problem-solving and critical thinking that would prove to save Project Apollo several times over. There was the incident that became known as “the Lauren error”: One day, her daughter Lauren, then four years old, was playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab when she somehow activated a pre-launch program, called P01, while the simulator was in midflight — which crashed the simulator altogether. Hamilton created a program add-on in the technical documentation warning users not to launch P01 during flight. She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake. Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish. Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program. This was an early example of “defensive” programming, the practice of building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own. Hamilton’s most famous contribution to the Apollo program came during the pivotal Apollo 11 mission to land on the moon in July of 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised the alarm. It had detected a 1202 error: The computer was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch, and it was possible the system would not be able to handle the complex landing procedure. But Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software, able to shut down unnecessary background tasks in order to prioritize mission-critical tasks. Houston trusted Hamilton’s software and allowed the mission to proceed, and two men walked on the moon for the first time. Later career and legacyHamilton continued to work at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s. As the Apollo program wound down, the Instrumentation Lab spun out of MIT to become the independent Draper Laboratory.“Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” says Jerry M. Wohletz SM ’97, PhD ’00, president and CEO at Draper. “Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.”Hamilton went on to create her first software company, Higher Order Software, in 1976. The firm was based on Hamilton’s software engineering approach of error prevention and fault tolerance. A decade later, Hamilton founded another software company, Hamilton Technologies, “to provide products and services to modernize the planning, system engineering and software development process in order to maximize reliability, lower cost and accelerate time to market.” Hamilton Technologies’ flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language and methodology for engineering complex software systems that prioritize error prevention and defensive programming. Throughout her career, Hamilton worked to achieve recognition for software engineering as a dedicated discipline. “I fought to bring the software legitimacy so that it — and those building it — would be given its due respect, and thus I began to use the term ‘software engineering’ to distinguish it from hardware and other kinds of engineering, yet treat each type of engineering as part of the overall systems engineering process,” Hamilton told El Pais in 2018. “When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing. It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. Software eventually and necessarily gained the same respect as any other discipline.”Among her many awards and honors, Hamilton was recognized with the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for scientific and technical contributions in 2003; the Computer History Museum Fellow Award in 2017; the Intrepid Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019; and induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022.Later in life, Hamilton become an icon for women in science and technology, especially after a now-famous photo, showing her next to a printout of her MIT team’s Apollo code, began circulating online. In 2015, the Apollo software she helped to develop was added in its entirety to the code-sharing site GitHub. And in 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure after a set originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock, honoring her and several other women of NASA history, became available worldwide. “Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers. Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’” says de Weck. “She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from.” Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn. A memorial service will take place in the spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

comments.author: diskzero
comments.textRawHtml: I was able to meet her, and others who worked at the MIT Instrumentation/Draper Lab, as a start-up I was with received funding from a VC firm founded by other Draper Lab members from the Apollo era. I was totally out of my league talking with them. This was thirty years ago and I remember her talking about formalized control systems. It was fascinating but went totally over my head. My startup was a fairly silly multimedia CD-ROM company and I was just happy to be in the room.
comments.textZhHtml: 我能够见到她，以及在麻省理工学院仪器/德雷珀实验室工作的其他人，作为一家初创公司，我获得了来自阿波罗时代其他德雷珀实验室成员创立的风险投资公司的资金。我完全无法与他们交谈。那是三十年前的事了，我记得她谈论过形式化控制系统。这很令人着迷，但完全超出了我的想象。我的初创公司是一家相当愚蠢的多媒体 CD-ROM 公司，我很高兴能来到这个房间。

children.author: p4bl0
children.textRawHtml: Thanks for sharing this story from this point of view so genuinely. I really enjoyed it more than I thought I would enjoy any comments under this sad news.
children.textZhHtml: 感谢您如此真诚地从这个角度分享这个故事。我真的很喜欢它，比我想象的更喜欢在这个悲伤的消息下发表任何评论。

comments.author: Gravityloss
comments.textRawHtml:
I think projects like Apollo are important in a way that they let extraordinary people to use their capabilities.

I feel from personal experiences as well as from many close people that often the corporate world really struggles on dealing with talent. And I don't mean autistic savants doing obscure things but relatively normal but very competent people doing actual well based comprehensive business helping work - but you have to do something in a very dumbed down way because the organization is built in a way to only accept small changes to the state of the art.
comments.textZhHtml:
我认为像阿波罗这样的项目很重要，因为它们让非凡的人发挥他们的能力。

我从个人经历以及许多亲密的人那里感受到，企业界在与人才打交道方面往往确实很困难。我并不是说自闭症专家做一些晦涩的事情，而是相对正常但非常有能力的人做真正基础良好的综合业务帮助工作 - 但你必须以一种非常愚蠢的方式做一些事情，因为组织的建立方式只接受对最先进技术的微小改变。

children.author: PaulHoule
children.textRawHtml:
It's not just "can these organizations produce brilliant output?" but "can they produce quality output?" I think you can take a lot of pride in doing ordinary things properly and giving people good experiences.

I stayed at a major chain hotel this weekend and it was a fine stay, the staff was great, but... there were just numerous little tech problems. Like the USB chargers had bad connections so I plugged in my phone overnight and it didn't charge and the next morning I found I had to twist the connector to get it to work. And then when I tried to connect to the WiFi with a Steam Deck [1] it wanted my personal info to join their rewards program, but the complicated Javascript-based dropdown menu to pick a state barely worked and after a minute of screwing with it I was able to pick the wrong state but not pick my real state so I looked up a zip code in that state and entered it.

When I got home I got an email from "no-reply@thathotelchainfoundedbyparishiltonsgreatgrandfather.com" gushing about how they want me to have the perfect experience and how badly they want to hear from me. Like yeah, they want me to call their 800 number and give me a piece of my mind.

It bugs me because I spend my day fixing problems with Javascript apps and I know all about those overcomplicated dropdowns. I get the feeling that if a staff member screwed up they'd be held accountable but people act like technology problems are like the weather and there is nothing we can do about it.

[1] granted an unusual device BUT... I don't travel with a laptop anymore, don't need to connect my phone with WiFi in 5G country and may or may not connect my iPhone. They could have just used the <select> that comes with HTML and it would have "just worked" and today you have so many options to style those with CSS
children.textZhHtml:
这不仅仅是“这些组织能否产出出色的成果？”但“他们能产出高质量的成果吗？” 我认为你可以为正确地做平凡的事情并为人们提供良好的体验而感到自豪。

这个周末我住在一家大型连锁酒店，住得很愉快，工作人员很棒，但是……只是存在许多小技术问题。 就像 USB 充电器连接不良一样，所以我把手机插了一夜，但它没有充电，第二天早上我发现我必须扭转连接器才能让它工作。 然后，当我尝试使用 Steam Deck [1] 连接到 WiFi 时，它希望我的个人信息加入他们的奖励计划，但是用于选择州的复杂的基于 Javascript 的下拉菜单几乎不起作用，经过一分钟的操作，我能够选择错误的州，但无法选择我的真实州，所以我查找了该州的邮政编码并输入了它。

当我回到家时，我收到了一封来自“no-reply@thathotelchainfoundedbyparishiltonsgreatgrandfather.com”的电子邮件，滔滔不绝地讲述他们如何希望我拥有完美的体验以及他们多么希望收到我的来信。 是的，他们希望我拨打他们的 800 号码并告诉我我的想法。

这让我很烦恼，因为我整天都在解决 Javascript 应用程序的问题，而且我了解那些过于复杂的下拉菜单。 我的感觉是，如果一名工作人员搞砸了，他们会被追究责任，但人们的表现就像技术问题就像天气一样，我们对此无能为力。

[1] 授予了一个不寻常的设备，但是...我不再携带笔记本电脑旅行，不需要在 5G 国家/地区将我的手机连接到 WiFi，并且可能会也可能不会连接我的 iPhone。 他们本来可以只使用 HTML 附带的 <select> ，它就会“正常工作”，而今天您有很多选项可以使用 CSS 来设置样式

children.author: cmrdporcupine
children.textRawHtml:
Yeah, something like the Apollo project has an exciting and profound enough destination/vision that it acts like a forcing function that herds all the cats.

The thing I've taken away most from my multidecade career is that the hardest part is getting any group of people all marching in the same direction, of their own volition. Everyone's motivations always differ. And leadership that just tries to force one direction almost always fails to consider enough viewpoints. And the alternatives, a deliberate rhizomatic chaos, or cutthroat competition, can be entirely demoralizing.
children.textZhHtml:
是的，像阿波罗计划这样的事情有一个令人兴奋和深刻的目的地/愿景，它就像一个强迫功能，聚集了所有的猫。

我从数十年的职业生涯中得到的最大收获是，最困难的部分是让任何一群人都自愿朝着同一个方向前进。每个人的动机总是不同的。仅仅试图强行推动一个方向的领导层几乎总是无法考虑足够的观点。还有其他选择，故意的根茎混乱，或者残酷的竞争， 可能会让人彻底士气低落。

children.author: _russross
children.textRawHtml:
I always take time to look at those photos when I see them making the rounds.

Such a brilliant person, such an incredible body of work. And yet she indulges in a fun and silly photo shoot. It's a wonderful moment of humanity, and a reminder that the history of computer science is fundamentally about people.
children.textZhHtml:
当我看到这些照片流传时，我总是会花时间看它们。

如此才华横溢的人，如此令人难以置信的作品。然而她却沉迷于拍摄有趣而愚蠢的照片。这是人类的一个美好时刻，并提醒我们计算机科学的历史从根本上讲是关于人的。

children.author: penskymaterial
children.textRawHtml: Little did she know, the term would be co-opted by guys changing the color of a button on a web site.
children.textZhHtml: 她几乎不知道，这个词会被那些改变网站按钮颜色的人所采用。

children.author: doginasuit
children.textRawHtml: And gate-kept by just as many. I wonder what she'd take more issue with. My understanding is she wanted to elevate people who work on software, not draw a line around it.
children.textZhHtml: 并由同样多的人看守。我想知道她会更关注什么。我的理解是，她想提升从事软件工作的人，而不是划清界限。

children.author: Dylan16807
children.textRawHtml:
If I had the option I would prefer the term "engineer" be gatekept.

Terminology can help elevate something that's often overlooked, but if every programmer gets called a "software engineer" there's no way to distinguish the special stuff.
children.textZhHtml:
如果可以选择，我更希望“工程师”这个词被保留下来。

术语可以帮助提升经常被忽视的东西，但如果每个程序员都被称为“软件工程师”，那么就没有办法区分特殊的东西。

children.author: ifwinterco
children.textRawHtml:
It is a protected title in some countries but not the UK (and I don’t think the US either?).

I believe in some European countries you’re not allowed to call yourself any kind of “Engineer” without being a member of a professional body?

So ironically if that was the case Margaret Hamilton would not have been allowed to coin the term
children.textZhHtml:
它在某些国家/地区是受保护的头衔，但在英国不是（我认为美国也不是？）。

我相信在某些欧洲国家，如果不是专业机构的成员，则不允许称自己为任何类型的“工程师”？

讽刺的是，如果是这样的话，玛格丽特·汉密尔顿就不会被允许创造这个词

children.author: doginasuit
children.textRawHtml:
It is not a protected title in the U.S., China, or India, and yet you could say those are three countries most responsible for writing the software that the rest of the world uses. I would argue there is some connection.

It is easy to see how gatekeeping is particularly valuable for those with the means to distinguish themselves. But for the rest of us, people who want to work on or consume a product, does a field benefit more from having an open gate or closed?
children.textZhHtml:
它在美国、中国或印度不受保护，但您可以说这三个国家对编写世界其他地区使用的软件负有最大责任。我认为两者之间存在某种联系。

很容易看出，对于那些有能力脱颖而出的人来说，守门是特别有价值的。但对于我们其他人，想要开发或消费产品的人来说，一个领域是从开放的大门还是封闭的大门中获益更多？

children.author: II2II
children.textRawHtml: If the title is backed by professional standards, standards by which someone can lose the title and be held legally liable, then I can see the gatekeeping as valuable. If it is used to restrict who can write software, then I would see it as detrimental.
children.textZhHtml: 如果该头衔得到专业标准的支持，按照这些标准，某人可能会失去该头衔并承担法律责任，那么我可以认为把关是有价值的。如果它被用来限制谁可以编写软件，那么我会认为这是有害的。
